artiest/chris-barber.text:
Donald Christopher Barber (1930 to 2021) was an English jazz musician, best known as a bandleader and trombonist. He was born in Welwyn Garden City and had violin lessons as a child. After the war he went to jazz clubs in London and studied at the Guildhall School of Music, where he met Alexis Korner, among others. In 1950 he founded an amateur band to play trad jazz and blues. He had trained as an actuary, but in 1951 he left his job at an insurance office, and in 1952 he became a professional musician.

At the end of 1952 he formed a band with the clarinettist Monty Sunshine that played in London clubs. After a performance in Copenhagen in 1953 it grew into his own group. Lonnie Donegan played in that band, and his appearances with Barber sparked the skiffle craze of the mid-1950s. Donegan had his first hit in America with Rock Island Line while he was still playing with Barber. In 1959 Barber himself reached the British top twenty with Petite Fleur. Later he recorded albums with Lonnie Donegan and with Louis Jordan, among others.

Barber gave a stage to blues singers such as Ottilie Patterson, for a time his wife, and brought African American blues musicians to Britain. In doing so he played an important part in the emergence of British rhythm and blues and the beat boom of the 1960s. His own music remained traditional New Orleans jazz, but his band became a breeding ground for the pop that came after it.
artiest/chris-barber.listen: Listen to Petite Fleur and notice the soft clarinet that carries the melody, with the band beneath it. Try to hear how this piece sounds like traditional jazz and yet was a hit.

artiest/chris-cornell.text:
Chris Cornell was born in Seattle in 1964 as Christopher John Boyle. After his parents divorced he took his mother's surname. As a child he had piano and guitar lessons, and between the ages of nine and eleven he listened endlessly to a pile of Beatles records he had found in a basement. As a teenager he struggled with depression and anxiety, and found something to hold on to in music. His mother bought him a snare drum, and that is how it began.

In 1984 he founded Soundgarden with Kim Thayil and Hiro Yamamoto. At first he sang and drummed at the same time; later he stood at the front alone. Soundgarden became the first grunge band to sign with a major label. With Badmotorfinger in 1991 and Superunknown the band grew, alongside Nirvana, Pearl Jam and Alice in Chains, into one of the great groups of Seattle. The music was heavy and slow, with influences from metal and Black Sabbath, and unusual time signatures.

Cornell had a range of almost four octaves and a powerful, soaring way of singing. He also founded Temple of the Dog, as a tribute to his late friend Andrew Wood, and later sang in Audioslave. As a solo artist he made Euphoria Mourning, among other albums, and he sang You Know My Name for the James Bond film Casino Royale. He died in 2017, shortly after a Soundgarden concert in Detroit. He is regarded as one of the most important voices of grunge.
artiest/chris-cornell.listen: Listen to Jesus Christ Pose by Soundgarden. Notice the heavy, thundering guitars and drums, and how Cornell rises above them with high, soaring cries.

artiest/chris-dave.text:
Chris Dave, nicknamed Daddy, is a drummer, composer and bandleader from Houston, Texas. He began playing in church at the end of the 1980s and names jazz as his strongest influence. As a teenager he listened with his father to jazz greats such as Miles Davis and John Coltrane. He studied at the Houston High School for the Performing and Visual Arts and then at Howard University in Washington, where he met the producers Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis. That led to the start of his professional career with the R&B group Mint Condition.

He played as a gospel drummer with the Winans family and reached a jazz audience through his work with the saxophonist Kenny Garrett, on whose album Standard of Language he can be heard. He then became a member of the Robert Glasper Experiment and played on Adele's Grammy-winning album 21. He also played on D'Angelo's album Black Messiah and went on a world tour with him. He further played in Bilal's live band and on Jill Scott's tour in 2008. Under his own name he released Cuffin Season and Smoke Break in 2020 and Thine People in 2021.

Dave is known for his virtuoso stick technique and his strong feeling for syncopation, rhythms that go against the beat. He moves between jazz, gospel and hip-hop. His playing shows how jazz drummers have changed the rhythm of R&B and hip-hop in the twenty-first century.
artiest/chris-dave.listen: Listen to a track from Adele's album 21 or from Black Messiah and notice the drums. Try to hear how the rhythm falls just ahead of or behind the beat, so that the groove sounds loose and yet alive.

artiest/chris-lowe.text:
Chris Lowe is an English keyboard player and songwriter, born in Blackpool in 1959. He grew up in a musical family: his grandfather was a trombonist. Lowe learned trombone and piano and as a boy played in a dance orchestra and a brass band. At the end of the 1970s he became a fan of disco. Even so he chose security and went to study architecture in Liverpool.

During a work placement in London in 1981 he met Neil Tennant in a shop selling sound equipment. They discovered that they both loved electronic music and began writing songs together. That is how the Pet Shop Boys came about. In 1985 the duo broke through with West End Girls, and in 1985 Lowe also gave up his studies for good. Hits such as It's a Sin, Always on My Mind and Go West followed. Lowe wrote a large part of the accompaniment and often the melodies too, while Tennant wrote the lyrics and sang.

Lowe is the man behind the dance floor in the sound of the Pet Shop Boys. He followed what was happening in clubs, first in the gay clubs of London and later in Ibiza and Berlin, and brought it into their synth-pop. On stage he stands almost motionless behind his keyboards, wearing a cap and sunglasses. The Pet Shop Boys became the most successful duo in British pop history.
artiest/chris-lowe.listen: Listen to West End Girls by the Pet Shop Boys. Notice Chris Lowe's calm synthesizer pattern beneath Neil Tennant's spoken verse, which is almost a rap.

artiest/chris-martin.text:
Chris Martin was born in Exeter, Devon, in 1977 and is an English singer, pianist, songwriter and producer. He is best known as the singer and co-founder of the rock band Coldplay. He grew up as the eldest of five children, lived with his family in Zimbabwe at the age of ten, and went to Sherborne School, where he met Phil Harvey, later Coldplay's manager. There he was president of the Sting fan club and played in a blues band with Harvey. At University College London he studied Greek and Latin and graduated with the highest honours.

In 1996 he met Jonny Buckland during freshers' week. They came up with the idea of a band and from early 1997 wrote their first songs. Guy Berryman joined, followed by the drummer Will Champion. At first they were called Big Fat Noises and then Starfish, before the name Coldplay came about. The band broke through worldwide with the album Parachutes in 2000 and the albums that followed. As a member of Coldplay, Martin won seven Grammys and nine Brit Awards. According to the source, the group is among the most successful of the twenty-first century.

Martin writes songs built around piano and guitar, with singing that ranges from a whisper to high and exuberant. His lyrics are often about longing, comfort and hope. Coldplay made a form of stadium pop that is emotional and accessible. Martin is the face of the group, and he also writes for other artists.
artiest/chris-martin.listen: Listen to a track from Parachutes and notice the piano and Martin's high, vulnerable voice. Try to hear how softly the song begins and how the band slowly joins in.

artiest/chris-mcgregor.text: The pianist Chris McGregor grew up in the Transkei, where his father was a missionary, and studied in Cape Town. In the early 1960s he formed The Blue Notes, a group with Black musicians such as the saxophonist Dudu Pukwana and the drummer Louis Moholo. A mixed band was almost impossible under apartheid. In 1964 the group played at the Antibes festival and stayed in Europe, first in Zurich and then in London. There in 1970 McGregor founded the big band Brotherhood of Breath, which mixed township melodies, kwela and free improvisation. Later he lived in France, where he died in 1990.
artiest/chris-mcgregor.listen: Hear how cheerful township melodies turn into wild collective improvisation.

artiest/chris-stein.text:
Chris Stein was born in Brooklyn in 1950 and is an American guitarist and songwriter, a co-founder of the new wave band Blondie. He grew up in the Midwood neighbourhood and was expelled from his high school because of his long hair. In 1973 he became the guitarist of the Stillettoes, where he began a relationship with the singer Debbie Harry. In the summer of 1974 Stein, Harry and the rhythm section left that group to start their own band. That became Blondie, a fixture of the punk and new wave scene around CBGB and Max's Kansas City. At the end of the 1970s the group achieved international fame.

Stein wrote many hits with Debbie Harry, including Heart of Glass, Dreaming, Island of Lost Souls, Rapture and Rip Her to Shreds. Sunday Girl he wrote alone. From 1978 to 1982 he presented the public-access TV programme TV Party. Blondie split up in 1982 and reunited in 1997. He also produced and played on the soundtrack of the hip-hop film Wild Style in 1982 and wrote the music for the 1980 film Union City. Between 1982 and 1984 he ran the label Animal Records.

Stein is also a photographer. He documented the early punk scene of New York, with Debbie Harry and Blondie, and worked with artists such as Andy Warhol and H.R. Giger. His book Negative appeared in 2014. His guitar playing and songs connect punk, pop and disco, and with Wild Style he also stands at the cradle of early hip-hop film.
artiest/chris-stein.listen: Listen to Heart of Glass and notice the tight, danceable beat and the light guitar lines beneath it. Try to hear how the band joins punk and disco in a single song.

artiest/chris-thile.text:
Chris Thile was born in Oceanside, California, in 1981 and is an American singer, mandolinist, composer and radio presenter. He grew up in a musical family. At the age of five he began playing the mandolin, with lessons from John Moore, whose bluegrass band he had heard as a child in a pizzeria. At the age of eight his family formed the band Nickel Creek together with the Watkins family. Their first album, Little Cowpoke, was released at the end of 1993. Later came Nickel Creek and This Side, which won a Grammy for best contemporary folk album. In 2005 Why Should the Fire Die? was released.

Under his own name Thile made solo records, such as Not All Who Wander Are Lost in 2001 and Deceiver in 2004, on which he wrote, sang and played all the parts himself. In 2008 an album with the bassist Edgar Meyer was released, and in 2013 the first volume of Bach: Sonatas and Partitas. He also plays in Punch Brothers, an acoustic folk and bluegrass quintet. In 2012 he received a MacArthur Fellowship. From 2016 to 2020 he presented the radio programme Live from Here.

His music moves between bluegrass, folk, classical and pop. Thile shows that a mandolin can be a versatile solo instrument, and that bluegrass has more room than its tradition suggests. Nickel Creek and Punch Brothers brought bluegrass to a new, wide audience.
artiest/chris-thile.listen: Listen to a track by Nickel Creek and notice the fast mandolin that carries the melody, with fiddle and guitar around it. Try to hear how the three instruments take turns.

artiest/christine-schafer.text:
Christine Schäfer was born in Frankfurt in 1965 and is a German operatic soprano. From 1984 to 1991 she studied at the Hochschule der Künste in Berlin, with Aribert Reimann and Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, among others, and attended masterclasses with Arleen Augér and Sena Jurinac. After her studies she sang at the opera house in Innsbruck. In 1993 she made her American debut as Sophie in Der Rosenkavalier in San Francisco. In 1995 she made her mark at the Salzburg Festival in the title role of Berg's Lulu, a part she later also sang at the Metropolitan Opera and at Glyndebourne.

Her repertoire runs from Baroque operas and Bach cantatas to the great Mozart roles, such as Konstanze, Cherubino and Pamina. She also sang modern works such as Pierrot Lunaire and Pli selon pli, which she recorded with Pierre Boulez. Her recordings further include songs by Robert Schumann, with which she won a Gramophone Award in 1997, songs by Schubert, including Winterreise, and songs by Chausson and Debussy. Early recordings are Messe h-Moll from 1994 and Der Freischütz from 1996. In 1998 she recorded a recital of Mozart and Richard Strauss with Claudio Abbado. In 2014 she took a sabbatical that was later extended indefinitely.

Since 2015 she has been professor of voice at the Hochschule für Musik Hanns Eisler in Berlin. Her voice is clear and agile, and she combines dramatic power with precision in song interpretation. She shows that an opera singer can also be at home in small, intimate songs.
artiest/christine-schafer.listen: Listen to a Schumann song in her performance and notice how softly and precisely she shapes each phrase, with only a piano beside her. Try to hear how the words guide the melody.

artiest/christoph-eschenbach.text:
Christoph Eschenbach was born in 1940 in Breslau, now Wrocław, and is a German pianist and conductor. Orphaned by the war, he was raised by a cousin of his mother, who gave him piano lessons from 1948. At the age of eleven he saw Wilhelm Furtwängler conduct, an experience that made a deep impression on him. He studied piano and conducting at the Musikhochschule in Cologne and later in Hamburg. In 1962 he won the ARD piano competition, and a year later the Clara Haskil Competition in Vevey. In 1964 he made his first recording for Deutsche Grammophon, of music by Mozart. As a conductor he worked for more than three years with George Szell, among others.

On record he released music for piano and for four hands in the 1970s, such as Préludes in 1972 and Four Hand Piano Music in 1973 and 1975, and in 1978 the first volumes of a series of songs in which he accompanied singers. Over the years he was chief conductor of thirteen orchestras worldwide. In 2014 he won a Grammy for an album of works by Paul Hindemith, and in 2015 he received the Ernst von Siemens Music Prize for his services to music.

Eschenbach is an example of the musician who moved from the piano to the conductor's podium. As a conductor he gave well-known symphonic works room for slow tempos and plenty of expression. He also played a role as a teacher and mentor of young musicians. His long career shows how the classical tradition of German music is handed down.
artiest/christoph-eschenbach.listen: Listen to a recording of Mozart's Sonata in D Major, K. 448, for two pianos and notice how the two pianists take up each other's melodies. Try to hear how the questions and answers between the two grand pianos sound.

artiest/christophe-beck.text: Christophe Beck was born in Montreal in 1968. He studied at Yale University and then film composition at the University of Southern California, under Jerry Goldsmith, among others. His breakthrough was the music for the second season of the television series Buffy the Vampire Slayer, which won him an Emmy. After that he worked a great deal on comedies, such as the Hangover films (2009–2013). For Disney he wrote the instrumental score of Frozen (2013) and Frozen II (2019). For Frozen he received an Annie Award. For Marvel he wrote the three Ant-Man films and the series WandaVision and Hawkeye (both 2021). He works from Santa Monica, California.
artiest/christophe-beck.listen: Notice how in Frozen he uses orchestra and choir for the fairy-tale atmosphere, and how in Ant-Man he sets a short, rhythmic hero motif in the brass.

artiest/christopher-franke.text:
Christopher Franke was born in 1953 and is a German film composer and pioneer of electronic music. He studied composition at the Berlin conservatoire, with Karlheinz Stockhausen and John Cage as influences. From 1970 to 1987 he was a member of Tangerine Dream. There he was nicknamed the Sequencer King, because he used an analogue sequencer on stage. His work with sequencers is considered decisive for the group's fast, hypnotic style, among other things on the album Phaedra from 1973, which paved the way for the classic Tangerine Dream sound and for the Berlin school.

With Tangerine Dream he wrote music for films such as Sorcerer, Thief, Risky Business and Legend. After his departure he pursued a solo career. In 1991 he opened a studio in West Hollywood and wrote film music for, among others, Universal Soldier, Tarzan and the Lost City and Night of the Running Man. His first solo album, Pacific Coast Highway, was released in 1991, followed by Klemania and Raven in 1993. A year later he founded the label Sonic Images. For television he wrote the music for the science fiction series Babylon 5.

His music consists of synthesizers and rhythmic sequencer lines, sometimes with orchestral colours. Franke brought the electronic sound of the Berlin school to American film and television. In doing so he belongs to the musicians who gave synthesizer music a permanent place in film music.
artiest/christopher-franke.listen: Listen to Phaedra by Tangerine Dream and notice the pulsing sequencer that runs beneath the music like a stream of short notes. Try to hear how the sounds change slowly without a clear song emerging.

artiest/christopher-maltman.text:
Christopher Maltman was born in Cleethorpes in 1970 and is a British operatic baritone who performs internationally. He studied biochemistry at the University of Warwick, then music at the Royal Academy of Music, and trained with British Youth Opera. In 1997 he won the Lieder Prize at the BBC Cardiff Singer of the World Competition. The same year he made his debut at the Royal Opera in London, where he has since sung more than fifteen leading roles, including Papageno in Die Zauberflöte, Count Almaviva in Le nozze di Figaro and Guglielmo in Così fan tutte.

In the great opera houses of Europe and North America he specialised in the Italian dramatic baritone repertoire, above all Verdi's Rigoletto, but also Rodrigo in Don Carlo, Simon Boccanegra and Ford in Falstaff. In 2019 he sang the title role of Enescu's Œdipe at the Salzburg Festival, and in 2020 Jochanaan in Richard Strauss's Salome in Frankfurt. One reviewer praised his sturdy yet lyrical voice. He made many recordings of song repertoire, including Schumann's Dichterliebe with Graham Johnson, a Debussy album with Malcolm Martineau and English songs with Roger Vignoles. He also sang in Vaughan Williams's Serenade to Music and in A Sea Symphony in 2003.

Maltman is known as a singer who masters both the dramatic opera stage and the chamber music of song. His recordings of English songs keep alive a tradition that is little known outside Britain. His work shows that the story in a song can be told in a way that is both theatrical and intimate.
artiest/christopher-maltman.listen: Listen to his recording of Schumann's Dichterliebe and notice how the piano and the voice follow each other. Try to hear how the singer gives each song its own colour and mood.

artiest/chu-berry.text:
Leon Brown Chu Berry (1908 to 1941) was an American jazz tenor saxophonist of the 1930s. He was born in Wheeling, West Virginia, and studied for three years at West Virginia State College. He began on alto saxophone with local bands and switched to tenor after hearing Coleman Hawkins on tour. According to the critic Gary Giddins, he got his nickname because he chewed on the mouthpiece of his saxophone or because he had a Fu Manchu moustache.

His career took place mainly in swing bands: first with Sammy Stewart, then with Benny Carter, Teddy Hill and Fletcher Henderson. His best-known period was the one with Cab Calloway from 1937 to 1941, where he is said to have turned the orchestra into a real jazz orchestra. As a sideman he played on recordings by Bessie Smith, Mildred Bailey, Teddy Wilson, Billie Holiday and Lionel Hampton. He wrote Christopher Columbus, with lyrics by Andy Razaf, recorded in 1936 by Henderson's orchestra. The song grew into one of the most popular riff tunes of the swing era and returned in Jimmy Mundy's arrangement of Sing, Sing, Sing for Benny Goodman.

Between 1934 and 1939, when Hawkins was playing in Europe, Berry was among the younger tenor players who competed for the lead, alongside Ben Webster and Lester Young. His command of advanced harmony influenced Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker. Parker named his first son Leon after him. Berry also took part in jam sessions at Minton's Playhouse, which helped bebop come into being. He died in 1941 at a young age.
artiest/chu-berry.listen: Listen to Christopher Columbus in the version by Fletcher Henderson and notice the short, repeated riff of the orchestra. Try to hear how the saxophone solos above the band.

artiest/chubby-checker.text:
Chubby Checker, born Ernest Evans in 1941, is an American rock and roll singer and dancer. He was born in South Carolina and grew up in the South Philadelphia neighbourhood. At eleven he formed a vocal group on the street, and at school he imitated Elvis Presley, Jerry Lee Lewis and Fats Domino. His boss at the greengrocer's market gave him the nickname Chubby. Through the owner of a poulterer's and the lyricist Kal Mann he got a private recording to Dick Clark, the host of American Bandstand. Clark's wife came up with the name Chubby Checker, after Fats Domino.

His big breakthrough came in 1960 with his version of The Twist, an R&B song by Hank Ballard & The Midnighters. It became the most popular single since the start of the Billboard Hot 100 in 1960, and remained so in the rankings of 2008 and 2013. In 1961 came Pony Time with the Pony dance and Let's Twist Again, his biggest hit in Britain. In 1962 he popularised Limbo Rock, an instrumental by The Champs to which he added lyrics and the limbo dance. He also released other dances such as the Fly. He made albums such as Twist With Chubby Checker and For Twisters Only in 1960.

Checker's music is simple and rhythmic: a tight beat, short phrases and lyrics that dictate the dance. He showed that a dance could make a hit, and that a song could be a movement. In 2014 he was inducted into the National Rhythm & Blues Hall of Fame, and in 2025 he was selected for the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/chubby-checker.listen: Listen to The Twist and notice the short, repeated phrases and the tight rhythm. Try to hear how the lyrics almost describe the dance, so that you can join in without any explanation.

artiest/chuck-berry.text:
Chuck Berry was born in St. Louis, Missouri, in 1926, as Charles Edward Anderson Berry. He is one of the Black pioneers of rock 'n' roll, alongside Fats Domino, Little Richard and Bo Diddley. Berry made the electric guitar the main instrument of the new music, and he wrote his own lyrics about cars, school and teenagers who dreamed of another life.

In May 1955 the bluesman Muddy Waters advised him to go to Leonard Chess, of the label Chess Records in Chicago. That same year Maybellene was released, an adaptation of the old country tune Ida Red. It reached number 1 on Billboard's rhythm and blues chart. Roll Over Beethoven (1956), Rock and Roll Music (1957), Sweet Little Sixteen and Johnny B. Goode (1958) followed. His style was a blend: the riffs of jump blues, the storytelling of country, the tempo of rhythm and blues. On stage he did his duckwalk, hopping across the stage in a crouch with the guitar in front of him.

The Beatles and The Rolling Stones recorded his songs, and his riffs became the foundation of rock guitar. When the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inducted its first names in 1986, Berry was among them. Johnny B. Goode is the only rock 'n' roll song on the Golden Record that travelled into space with the Voyager probes. How far the music travelled you can hear in Peter Tosh, who recorded the song as reggae in 1983. Berry died in 2017.
artiest/chuck-berry.listen: Johnny B. Goode begins not with singing but with a guitar intro. Berry borrowed it from Carl Hogan, the guitarist of Louis Jordan, and played it harder and with two strings at once (double stops). Listen to how those two-note chords give the riff a sharp, almost horn-like sound.

artiest/chuck-d.text:
Chuck D's real name is Carlton Douglas Ridenhour. He was born in 1960 on Long Island, near New York. At home Motown and show tunes were played. He studied graphic design at Adelphi University, where he met William Drayton, the future Flavor Flav. He hosted a hip-hop show on the radio and designed flyers for hip-hop parties.

In 1985 he founded the group Public Enemy with Flavor Flav. Rick Rubin heard the demo Public Enemy Number One and wanted the group for his label Def Jam straight away. Yo! Bum Rush the Show in 1987, It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back in 1988 and Fear of a Black Planet in 1990 followed. Well-known tracks are Bring the Noise, Fight the Power and Welcome to the Terrordome. The music was hard and full: layers of samples, sirens and loud beats sliding over one another.

Chuck D has a powerful, booming voice, which he copied from the rapper Melle Mel and from sports commentators. His lyrics deal with the disadvantaging of Black Americans, with politics and with the media. In doing so he helped create politically conscious hip-hop in the 1980s. Later he worked with rock musicians such as Sonic Youth and Anthrax, played in Prophets of Rage and spoke out in favour of the free sharing of music over the internet.
artiest/chuck-d.listen: Listen to Fight the Power by Public Enemy. Notice the stacks of samples and sounds playing at once, and the heavy, commanding voice of Chuck D, who raps straight through them.

artiest/chuckie.text:
Chuckie is the artist name of Clyde Sergio Narain, a DJ, rapper and producer who was born in Paramaribo, Suriname, in 1978. He grew up in Suriname and was influenced by the music of that country. When one of his friends became a DJ, his own interest grew as well. From the age of thirteen he experimented with remixes at home and built up a record collection of his own. At first he played at parties for friends and family. In 1993 he started as a DJ at the club Voltage in The Hague. In 2008 he was the opening act of Sensation in the Amsterdam ArenA, something he had already dreamed about as a visitor to the first Sensation.

Chuckie is regarded as a producer of so-called dirty trance, a movement built around lively urban club nights with dancing, bright lights and a participating crowd. The genre is characterised by high lead synths over Latin-flavoured rhythms and samples. His hits include Let the Bass Kick, Aftershock and Make Some Noise, which he made with Junxterjack. He made remixes for Michael Jackson, David Guetta, Enrique Iglesias and The Partysquad, among others, and produced for 50 Cent, Kesha and Akon. His work featured on the BBC Radio 1 show What's Hot in EDM? He has a label of his own, Dirty Dutch Music.

Chuckie's music shows how the Dutch dance scene took part in the worldwide EDM wave, with influences from Suriname and Latin America. He belongs to the generation of DJs who fused pop songs and club music into a single sound.
artiest/chuckie.listen: Listen to Let the Bass Kick and notice the high, sharp synthesizer line above the hard rhythm. Try to hear how the bass drum and the lead take turns before the track breaks loose.

artiest/cidinho-en-doca.text:
Cidinho & Doca is a Brazilian MC duo from Rio de Janeiro. Sidney da Silva, known as MC Cidinho, and Marcos Paulo de Jesus Peixoto, MC Doca, both grew up in Cidade de Deus, a favela with a lot of crime. They have known each other since childhood and went to the same school. In 1994 they broke through, after the MCs Juniór & Leonardo asked them to sing the chorus of their song Rap das Armas. Those two had written the song a year earlier, but they recorded a version with new lyrics with Cidinho and Doca. The chorus imitates the sound of a machine gun and for that reason quickly stuck in the mind.

The duo belong to funk carioca, the hip-hop variant from Rio, and specifically to the subgenre proibidão, strictly forbidden funk. Such songs are often not played on the radio, because the lyrics seem to condone crime. A year later, in 1995, they made Rap da felicidade, on the album Eu só quero é ser feliz, in which they address social problems in the favelas. In 2008 Rap das Armas became known in Europe when it was used in a Brazilian film. Many DJs made a remix of it, and in several European countries, such as Sweden and the Netherlands, a remix reached the charts.

Cidinho & Doca show how a local genre from a Brazilian favela reached European dance floors through films and remixes. Their work is at once about life in the favela and about the reputation that life has.
artiest/cidinho-en-doca.listen: Listen to Rap das Armas and notice the chorus that imitates the sound of a machine gun. Try to hear how the solid funk rhythm carries the song and how the two MCs trade lines.

artiest/cidinho-en-doca-en-dj-marlboro.text:
Cidinho and Doca are MC Cidinho and MC Doca, a Brazilian funk duo from the world of funk carioca, the dance music of the favelas of Rio de Janeiro. They are counted among the best-known singers of proibidão, songs that by a court ruling may not be played on the radio, because according to the judge they would glorify crime. The duo were popular in 1994 with the song Rap da Felicidade.

DJ Marlboro played a key role in the movement. In 1989 he produced the compilation Funk Brasil, which is regarded as the starting point of funk carioca. The movement was then confirmed by a series of albums and songs. Cidinho and Doca later also made their own version of Rap das Armas, originally by Júnior e Leonardo, with adapted lyrics. That version became an international hit in 2008 and 2009, after the song had been heard in the film Tropa de Elite in 2007. Remixes, such as that by the Dutch DJ Quintino, reached number one in the Netherlands and Sweden in 2009.

Funk carioca is based on hard, minimalist drum machine rhythms, often with samples from Miami bass, and on raps in Brazilian Portuguese. The duo and DJ Marlboro show how a street music from Rio grew into a sound recognised worldwide.
artiest/cidinho-en-doca-en-dj-marlboro.listen: Listen to Rap da Felicidade. Notice the hard, repeating beat and how the raps race through it with plenty of rhythm.

artiest/circle.text:
Circle is a Finnish experimental rock band from Pori, founded around 1991. The bassist and singer Jussi Lehtisalo is the only member who has been there all those years. Their style is eclectic and constantly changing, and is associated with krautrock, heavy metal, progressive rock and ambient. On some albums they call themselves the New Wave of Finnish Heavy Metal. Their debut album Meronia from 1994 sounded like krautrock and had lyrics in an invented language. Many albums followed in quick succession, including Hissi and Zopalki in 1996 and Fraten in 1997.

International attention came with three albums: Andexelt in 1999, Prospekt in 2000 and Taantumus in 2001. From Sunrise in 2002 the core consists of Lehtisalo, keyboard player and singer Mika Rättö, drummer Tomi Leppänen and guitarist Janne Westerlund. Since then they have played heavier, metal-like music, which remains constantly influenced by the German krautrock band Faust. The members played in a great number of side projects, such as Pharaoh Overlord. In 2011 the group played the music live for the silent film Pori by Mika Taanila, which resulted in the album Suur-Pori. That same year they were artists in residence at the Dutch festival Roadburn. In 2017 their thirty-second album, Terminal, was released.

Circle shows that Finland has a rock scene of its own, with a mind of its own. The band plays repetitive, trance-like rhythms and heavy guitars, and blends genres without sticking to any rules.
artiest/circle.listen: Listen to a track from Prospekt and notice the repetitive rhythms and the heavy, tight guitar. Try to hear how the piece builds slowly instead of having a clear chorus.

artiest/cissy-houston.text:
Cissy Houston was born in 1933 as Emily Drinkard in Newark, New Jersey, the youngest of eight children. When her mother suffered a stroke, her father had the children sing hymns together. That is how the family group that later became known as the Drinkard Singers came about. Cissy sang in it from the age of five. In 1951 the group turned professional and she appeared at Carnegie Hall, and in 1957 she performed at the Newport Jazz Festival. A Joyful Noise from 1958 was one of the first gospel albums on a major label.

From the 1960s Houston became a much sought-after backing singer. In 1967 she founded the Sweet Inspirations, a women's group that sang behind Aretha Franklin and Elvis Presley. From 1970 she worked as a solo artist. She was the first to record Midnight Train to Georgia, which later became famous in the version by Gladys Knight, and she scored with I'll Be There and the dance track Think It Over. Later she won two Grammys for traditional gospel albums.

All her life she remained connected to the church: for more than fifty years she directed the music at the New Hope Baptist Church in Newark. She was the aunt of Dionne and Dee Dee Warwick and the mother of Whitney Houston. Through her the powerful gospel singing of the Black church flowed into soul and pop. You can hear it again in her daughter's voice. Cissy Houston died in 2024.
artiest/cissy-houston.listen: Listen to Midnight Train to Georgia in the version by Cissy Houston. Notice how her voice comes from the church: full, with soaring cries and ornaments, even in a pop song.

artiest/claire-pichet.text:
Claire Pichet is a French singer and musician who performs solo. She is best known for the song Summer 78, which she sang for the soundtrack of the 2003 film Good Bye Lenin! She worked with Yann Tiersen, the French multi-instrumentalist and composer, on the song Rue des cascades from 1996. That collaboration brought her into the world of French film music and small-scale chanson.

Under her own name the albums Rue des cascades in 1996, Le Phare in 1998, Black Session and Tout est calme in 1999 and C'était ici in 2002 were released, among others. She sings in French and also took part in the soundtrack of the film The Dreamlife of Angels.

Little is known about her life, and for that reason her place in pop history remains modest. Her importance lies mainly in the work around Tiersen and in the way Summer 78 reached a large audience outside France through Good Bye Lenin!
artiest/claire-pichet.listen: Listen to Summer 78 and notice the soft singing and the restrained accompaniment. Try to hear how a simple melody in a film can evoke a feeling of nostalgia.

artiest/clara-rockmore.text:
Clara Rockmore (1911 to 1998) was a classical violin prodigy and a virtuoso of the theremin, an electronic instrument that is played without touch. She was born in Vilnius, then part of the Russian Empire, into a Lithuanian-Jewish family. She was the sister of the pianist Nadia Reisenberg. At the age of four she became the youngest student ever at the St Petersburg conservatoire, where she studied with the violinist Leopold Auer. After the October Revolution the family moved back to Vilnius and then to Warsaw, before leaving for the United States in 1921. There she studied at the Curtis Institute of Music.

As a teenager she developed tendinitis in her bowing arm, which made her give up the violin. After meeting Léon Theremin she got to know his instrument and became its best-known player. She performed with orchestras in New York and Philadelphia and toured from coast to coast with Paul Robeson. She also helped Theremin refine his instrument. Not until 1977 did her first commercial record appear, The Art of the Theremin, produced by Bob Moog and Shirleigh Moog, with her sister Nadia on piano. In 2006 Clara Rockmore's Lost Theremin Album followed.

Rockmore stressed mastery of body and emotion. In her view you had to hit not just a note but the centre of it, and you must not sway or shake, because that would change the tone. Her classical training gave her a purity of intonation that few other thereminists had. She showed that an electronic instrument can sound as singing as a violin.
artiest/clara-rockmore.listen: Listen to a track from The Art of the Theremin and notice the pure, smooth tone that floats through the air like a singing voice. Try to hear how fluidly the notes flow into one another, without you hearing keys or strings.

artiest/clara-schumann.text: Clara Wieck was trained as a piano virtuoso by her father and was already known throughout Europe as a teenager. In 1840 she married Robert Schumann against his will, and even as the mother of eight children she kept giving concerts. She was one of the first to play from memory and made known the music of Beethoven, her husband and later Brahms. Her Piano Trio in G minor from 1846 joins a classical form with Romantic warmth.
artiest/clara-schumann.listen: Listen to the opening of the Piano Trio and hear how violin and piano take turns with the sombre melody in G minor.

artiest/clarence-ashley.text:
Clarence Ashley, also known as Tom Ashley, was born in 1895 as Clarence Earl McCurry in Bristol, Tennessee. He grew up with his grandfather, who ran a boarding house in the little village of Shouns in the Appalachians, and took his surname. From his mother and aunts he learned old folk songs and ballads, and from the itinerant lumberjacks and railway workers who slept at the boarding house he learned many more. From 1911 he travelled every summer with a medicine show, a travelling show in which music and comedy were meant to sell medicine.

In 1928 he made his first recordings, with the Blue Ridge Mountain Entertainers and the Carolina Tar Heels, and from 1929 also solo. He played banjo in the clawhammer style, and guitar. He sang old ballads that had come over from England and Ireland, such as The Coo Coo Bird and House Carpenter, and murder ballads such as Naomi Wise. In 1933 he recorded Rising Sun Blues with the harmonica player Gwen Foster: the oldest known recording of the song that later became known as House of the Rising Sun.

The Depression of the 1930s put an end to recording, and he worked as a miner and a truck driver. Because his records were on Harry Smith's Anthology of American Folk Music, he was rediscovered around 1960. With Doc Watson he played at folk festivals such as Newport. In this way Ashley became a direct link between the old music of the Appalachians and the folk revival of the 1960s. He died in 1967.
artiest/clarence-ashley.listen: Listen to Rising Sun Blues by Clarence Ashley and Gwen Foster from 1933. Notice the simple accompaniment and the harmonica, and compare the melody with the later versions of House of the Rising Sun.

artiest/clarence-ashley-en-doc-watson.text:
Clarence Ashley, born Clarence Earl McCurry in 1895 in Bristol, Tennessee, grew up with his grandfather in Shouns, a hamlet in the Appalachians. His grandfather bought him a banjo when he was eight. His mother and aunts taught him old ballads, and from itinerant lumberjacks and railway workers he picked up songs and playing styles. From 1911 he performed in medicine shows, travelling shows where music and comedy were used to sell remedies.

In 1928 Ashley made his first recordings for Gennett, followed by records with the Carolina Tar Heels, among others, and solo for Columbia. On 6 September 1933 he recorded Rising Sun Blues with the harmonica player Gwen Foster, the oldest known recording of the song that later became world-famous as House of the Rising Sun. Ashley played clawhammer banjo, often in a tuning of his own that he called sawmill, and sang English and Irish ballads that had been handed down for generations in the Appalachians.

The Depression of the 1930s ended his recording career. He worked in the mine and later as a truck driver. During the folk revival of the late 1950s he was rediscovered, partly because Harry Smith had included his early recordings in the Anthology of American Folk Music. Ralph Rinzler brought him back onto the stage in 1960. Ashley now played together with the guitarist Doc Watson, who in those years began his own recording career at his side, and performed at Carnegie Hall and at the Newport Folk Festival. Jerry Garcia said that he learned clawhammer by listening to Ashley.
artiest/clarence-ashley-en-doc-watson.listen: Listen to Rising Sun Blues and notice how bare it sounds: a voice and a stringed instrument, without drums or amplification. Compare it in your mind with the well-known rock versions of House of the Rising Sun.

artiest/claude-debussy.text: Claude Debussy studied at the Paris Conservatoire and at the 1889 World's Fair fell under the spell of the Javanese gamelan. He let chords sound for their colour rather than their function and used whole-tone scales and old modes. His Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune from 1894 opens with a free flute solo that is often called the beginning of modern music. He himself disliked the label Impressionism.
artiest/claude-debussy.listen: Listen to the flute solo that opens the Prélude and hear how, without a fixed metre or key, it slowly slides downward and curls up again.

artiest/claude-thornhill.text:
Claude Thornhill (1908 to 1965) was an American pianist, arranger, composer and bandleader. He was already playing piano professionally at the age of eleven and studied at the Cincinnati conservatory and at the Curtis Institute in Philadelphia. As a young man he formed a travelling duo with the clarinettist Danny Polo. He began his career in Cleveland together with Artie Shaw, and in 1931 they went to New York together. There he played with Glenn Miller, Paul Whiteman, Benny Goodman and Billie Holiday, among others, and wrote arrangements for Maxine Sullivan and later for Judy Garland in Babes in Arms. In the mid-1930s he worked as an arranger and pianist for Andre Kostelanetz.

In 1939 he founded the Claude Thornhill Orchestra, with Polo as first clarinettist. It was a refined dance band that stood out for its excellent jazz musicians and for the arrangements of Thornhill and Gil Evans. The band played without vibrato, so that the sound of each instrument came out better, and Thornhill encouraged his musicians to develop a cool, Cool Jazz-like tone. The best-known recordings were Snowfall, A Sunday Kind of Love and Love for Love. He also wrote I Wish I Had You, which Billie Holiday and Fats Waller recorded. In 1942 he joined the navy and performed in the Pacific. In 1946 he got his orchestra together again, with Gerry Mulligan, among others.

His sound and unusual instrumentation served in part as a model for the Miles Davis nonet on Birth of the Cool. Thornhill is thus a link between the swing of the 1930s and the Cool Jazz of the 1950s.
artiest/claude-thornhill.listen: Listen to Snowfall and notice the soft, vibrato-free sound of the wind instruments. Try to hear how the band sounds like a soft, almost floating whole rather than a fierce big band.

artiest/claudio-abbado.text:
Claudio Abbado (1933 to 2014) was an Italian conductor and one of the leading conductors of his generation. He was born in Milan, the son of a violinist and professor at the Verdi Conservatoire, who was his first piano teacher. During the German occupation of Milan his mother was in prison because she had hidden a Jewish child. That strengthened his anti-fascist convictions. At the age of eleven he wrote Viva Bartók on a wall, to the displeasure of the Gestapo. As a young man he attended performances at La Scala and rehearsals under Toscanini and Furtwängler.

His career took him to the most important stages. He was music director of La Scala in Milan, chief conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic and of the London Symphony Orchestra, honorary guest conductor of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra and music director of the Vienna State Opera. He also founded the Lucerne Festival Orchestra, the Mahler Chamber Orchestra and the Orchestra Mozart and led the European Union Youth Orchestra. His early recordings from the 1960s include Prokofiev and Ravel with piano soloists, and later came a large number of symphonies and operas. He received the Ernst von Siemens Music Prize and became a senator for life in Italy.

Abbado was known as a conductor who listened to his musicians and took chamber music as his starting point. He liked working with young musicians and built orchestras that sounded like one large chamber music group. His influence on concert life in Europe was great, and his recordings are still a benchmark.
artiest/claudio-abbado.listen: Listen to a recording of a Prokofiev or Ravel concerto under Abbado and notice how the orchestra accompanies the soloist. Try to hear how light and transparent the sound of the orchestra remains.

artiest/claudio-monteverdi.text: Claudio Monteverdi first worked at the court of the Gonzagas in Mantua and then for thirty years as maestro di cappella of San Marco in Venice. He defended a new style in which the text governs the music and dissonances may grate when the words call for it. His L'Orfeo from 1607 is regarded as the first great opera, with an orchestra that he prescribed in detail. His madrigal books let you hear, step by step, the transition from Renaissance to Baroque.
artiest/claudio-monteverdi.listen: Listen to the Toccata from L'Orfeo: a festive fanfare on a single chord, with which the audience in Mantua was quietened in 1607.

artiest/claudio-simonetti.text:
Claudio Simonetti was born in 1952 and is an Italian musician and film composer. He is the keyboard player of the progressive rock band Goblin, which was originally called Cherry Five. He is the son of the composer and entertainer Enrico Simonetti and studied at the Santa Cecilia conservatoire in Rome. His models were Keith Emerson, Brian Auger, Rick Wakeman and Tony Banks. Since the 1970s he has specialised in music for Italian and American horror films.

He often worked with the director Dario Argento, on films such as Deep Red, Suspiria, Tenebrae, Phenomena, Demoni and Opera. He also wrote music for films by Lucio Fulci, Lamberto Bava, Ruggero Deodato and Sergio Martino, such as The New Barbarians in 1983 and The Versace Murder in 1998. From 1978 he set up electronic disco projects. In 1979 he formed a group with Giancarlo Meo around the singer Vivien Vee, whose song Give Me a Break became a minor hit on the American dance chart. In 1983 he was the central figure in the Italo disco group Crazy Gang. In 1999 he founded the metal band Daemonia, which plays new versions of Goblin songs. Albums under his name include Tenebre in 1982 and Demons in 1985.

His music brings together synthesizers, organs and rock in dark, menacing sounds. Simonetti made sure that horror film and progressive rock in Italy gained a sound of their own, and that sound remained influential for later horror scores.
artiest/claudio-simonetti.listen: Listen to the title theme of Suspiria and notice the menacing, high sounds and the whispering voices. Try to hear how the music runs through the scene as a pounding, restless rhythm.

artiest/clef-club-orchestra.text:
The Clef Club was a society, social centre and union for African American musicians in Harlem. James Reese Europe and a few colleagues founded it on 11 April 1910, to put Black musicians in touch with employers and better-paid jobs, at a time when the ordinary musicians' union was open only to white musicians. The office was across from Marshall's Hotel, a meeting place for Black musicians. In its first weeks the club already had more than a hundred and thirty-five members. It was a meeting place and a fraternity as well as an employment agency and a concert hall.

The Clef Club Orchestra grew out of a benefit evening to pay for office space. The orchestra was led by James Reese Europe and numbered more than a hundred musicians with a great variety of instruments. Besides violins, cellos, basses and wind instruments, the stage held mandolins, guitars, banjos and a large bass drum, sometimes with a male chorus and ten pianists. Between 1912 and 1915 the orchestra played at Carnegie Hall in New York, on the initiative of David Mannes, among others, who wanted a benefit concert for the Music Settlement School in Harlem. The first concert raised five thousand dollars and was well received, although the press sometimes wrote about it in a condescending way.

The orchestra showed that African American musicians could give a symphonic concert in a large hall. The club went under in the mid-1920s. The orchestra therefore stands at the beginning of the road that Black music travelled to the great stages, and it belongs to the prehistory of jazz.
artiest/clef-club-orchestra.listen: Listen to a recording of Deep River, one of the pieces from the first Carnegie Hall programme, and notice the choral singing and the melody. Try to hear how a spiritual can sound in a large, classical ensemble.

artiest/clemencic-consort.text:
The Clemencic Consort is an Austrian early music ensemble, founded in 1968 by René Clemencic. Clemencic was born in Vienna in 1928 and died in 2022. He was a composer, conductor, harpsichordist, clavichordist and recorder player and studied at the University of Vienna and then in France, the Netherlands and West Germany. He led the Capella Musica Antiqua and the Drama Musicum in Vienna. In 1958 he had already founded Musica Antiqua, which after 1959 was called Ensemble Musica Antiqua, to play early music on historical instruments.

In the 1970s and 1980s the Consort made many recordings for Harmonia Mundi. Best known is the Carmina Burana series, an edition of five LPs in the years 1974 to 1978, later reissued on three CDs in 1990. Other recordings are Les Cantigas De Santa Maria Vol. 2 from 1976, La Fête De L'âne from 1980, Missa Prolationum and Troubadores from 1985 and 1986, and Salve Regina and Stabat Mater from 1987. The repertoire runs from medieval songs and dances to Renaissance masses.

The Consort plays on instruments of the period itself, such as recorders and string instruments, with singing. In this way it brought medieval music to a wide audience, at a time when interest in early music was growing. Clemencic himself also composed, including oratorios and chamber operas, and in 1978 wrote the film music for Molière.
artiest/clemencic-consort.listen: Listen to a piece from Carmina Burana in the performance by the Clemencic Consort and notice the medieval instruments, such as flutes and strings, alongside the singing. Try to hear how the rhythm of the dance drives the music.

artiest/clemencic-consort-en-rene-clemen.text:
René Clemencic was born in Vienna in 1928 and died there in 2022 at the age of 94. He studied at the University of Vienna and deepened his studies further in France, the Netherlands and West Germany. He was a composer, conductor and harpsichordist, also played the clavichord and the recorder, and in Vienna led the Capella Musica Antiqua and the Drama Musicum, among others.

In 1958 Clemencic founded Musica Antiqua, which after 1959 was called Ensemble Musica Antiqua. The group played early music on instruments of the period itself, at a time when that approach was still new. In 1968 the Clemencic Consort followed. With that ensemble he recorded, between 1974 and 1977, a five-LP series of the Carmina Burana, the medieval songs from the monastery of Benediktbeuern, released by Harmonia Mundi France. Clemencic also wrote work of his own, such as the Missa Mundi for five voices and orchestra from 1981, the oratorio Kabbala in Hebrew and the oratorio Apokalypsis on the Greek text of the Book of Revelation.

In the course, the Consort represents the medieval troubadours. A chantar is a song by the Comtessa de Dia from the twelfth century, one of the few surviving songs by a female troubadour. Ensembles such as Clemencic's made sure that such songs sounded again, with the distinctive colour of old instruments and a vocal line that moves freely through the text.
artiest/clemencic-consort-en-rene-clemen.listen: Listen to A chantar and notice the melody that moves calmly up and down at the start, with only little accompaniment. Which instruments do you hear, and how do they leave room for the voice?

artiest/clementina-de-jesus.text:
Clementina de Jesus (1901 to 1987) was a Brazilian samba singer. She was born in Carambita, a district on the edge of Valença, south of Rio de Janeiro, and at the age of eight moved with her family to the Osvaldo Cruz district of Rio. For years she followed the samba school Portela, and in 1940, after her marriage, she went to the samba school Mangueira. For more than twenty years she worked as a maid. In 1963 the composer Hermínio Bello de Carvalho discovered her. He asked her to take part in the show Rosa de Ouro in several Brazilian state capitals and made her first record for Odeon.

Her professional career began only at the age of sixty-three. Her distinctive voice can be heard on Rosa de Ouro 1 in 1965, Clementina de Jesus in 1966, Rosa de Ouro 2 in 1967, Fala Mangueira! in 1968 and Marinheiro só in 1973, among others. She also recorded with well-known samba musicians such as Pixinguinha and João da Bahiana. In Brazil she was called Mamãe. Elton Medeiros sang about her in Clementina, cadê você?, and Clara Nunes in 1977 in a song by Candeia. In 1983 artists such as Paulinho da Viola, João Nogueira and Elizeth Cardoso celebrated her with a show at the Teatro Municipal in Rio.

Despite her late start and short career she is one of the most popular female singers in Brazil. She is known for her contribution to carnival music and because she identified with the poor. Her singing shows how samba from the Afro-Brazilian community keeps its roots in an older singing tradition.
artiest/clementina-de-jesus.listen: Listen to a track from her album Rosa de Ouro 1 and notice her raw, deep voice and the chorus that answers. Try to hear how call and response carry the song, with percussion beneath.

artiest/cleveland-orchestra.text:
The Cleveland Orchestra is an American orchestra from Cleveland, Ohio. It was founded in 1918 by the pianist and impresario Adella Prentiss Hughes, the businessman John L. Severance, Father John Powers, the critic Archie Bell and the violinist and conductor Nikolai Sokoloff, who became the first music director. The first concert was on 11 December 1918 at Grays Armory. The orchestra belongs to the Big Five, the five American orchestras that are often named as the best. Since 1931 it has played at Severance Hall. In 1921 it began children's concerts, a tradition that has continued, and in 1924 the first record appeared, an abridged version of Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture.

The great name in its history is George Szell, who became the fourth music director in 1946. He wanted to make the best symphony orchestra in America and replaced many musicians to do so. His contract gave him complete artistic control. In 1957 the orchestra made a first European tour, also behind the Iron Curtain. Szell had the acoustics of Severance Hall adapted with the Szell Shell, to make the sound more balanced. Records from his time include Symphonies nos. 40 & 41 in 1956, Dvořák's Symphony no. 5 From the New World in 1957 and the four symphonies of Schumann in 1959.

The orchestra is known for its precision and ensemble playing. The current music director is Franz Welser-Möst. The Cleveland Orchestra shows how an orchestra in an industrial city grew into a world name, through strict rehearsal and a sound of its own.
artiest/cleveland-orchestra.listen: Listen to Mozart's Symphonies nos. 40 & 41 under Szell and notice the tight ensemble playing of the strings. Try to hear how precisely the entries and chords coincide.

artiest/cliff-burton.text:
Cliff Burton was an American bassist, born in 1962 in Castro Valley, near San Francisco. Through his father he got to know classical music, and he had piano lessons. He began playing bass at thirteen, after his older brother had died, and sometimes practised six hours a day. He listened to classical, jazz, southern rock, country and blues, and to bassists such as Geezer Butler, Lemmy Kilmister and Phil Lynott.

In 1982 he played with the band Trauma at the Whisky a Go Go in Los Angeles. James Hetfield and Lars Ulrich of Metallica heard him and asked him to be their new bassist. Burton agreed on condition that the band moved to the Bay Area, and that is what happened. He played on Kill 'Em All from 1983, with his bass solo (Anesthesia) Pulling Teeth, and on Ride the Lightning from 1984, on which he co-wrote six of the eight songs. The opening of For Whom the Bell Tolls is often taken for guitar, but it is his bass. Master of Puppets from 1986 followed, the band's breakthrough.

Burton used effects pedals such as wah-wah and distortion, which was unusual for bassists, and you can hear his classical training in the melodic bass parts, for example in Orion. On 27 September 1986, a day after a concert in Stockholm, he was killed when the tour bus crashed. He was 24. He is still regarded as one of the most influential bassists in metal.
artiest/cliff-burton.listen: Listen to the opening of For Whom the Bell Tolls by Metallica. Notice the high, distorted run that sounds like a guitar: that is Cliff Burton's bass.
